name: Tibetan multi-herb formula (studied for intermittent claudication)
short: In four small trials, mild side effects (stomach discomfort, tiredness, skin eruption) were no more common than with placebo; evidence quality was very low and long-term effects are unknown.
text: A systematic review of a fixed Tibetan multi-herb preparation for intermittent claudication included five placebo-controlled trials with 365 participants, each with at least 16 weeks of follow-up. Mild side effects, especially gastrointestinal discomfort, tiredness and skin eruption, were reported, but their frequency did not differ from placebo (odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.83; four studies, 231 participants), which the reviewers rated as very low quality evidence; they concluded that side effects do not appear to be a problem but that the longer-term effects of treatment are unknown, and they noted small trials, relatively high withdrawal rates and evidence of publication bias. An earlier review of studies in peripheral arterial occlusive disease reported that serious adverse events were not related to the active treatment and that non-serious adverse events were as frequent as with placebo; the abstract does not say what the serious events were. A later overview found 29 trials (1 meta-analysis, 21 controlled trials and 7 open trials) and 3 retrospective case studies across different conditions, with a total of 1,704 patients given the formula (697 of them children), 333 given placebo and 394 untreated or healthy; it reported that dropouts and withdrawals were 2.5 and 3.5 times higher in the placebo group than in the formula group and concluded that the results suggest a favourable safety profile. The abstract does not say which studies these rates come from or how they were calculated; the totals mix controlled and open trials, and the formula and placebo groups are very unequal in size. These findings apply to the specific multi-herb product tested, not to its individual herbs. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
